deep.reconstruction:
Context: this is §2 (end) and the start of §3 of Riemann's 1861 Paris prize essay ('Commentatio mathematica…', received 1 July 1861). Section 1 on the previous page sets up equation (I), the heat equation in an inhomogeneous anisotropic body: sum_i d/dx_i ( sum_i' a_{i,i'} du/dx_i' ) = h du/dt.

§2 (cont.). The a_{i,i'}(x) are the resultant conductivities. h(x) is the heat capacity per unit volume (specific heat times density). Both are arbitrary given functions of x1, x2, x3. Riemann makes two assumptions:
(i) Conductivity is the same in opposite directions, so a_{i,i'} = a_{i',i} (the matrix a is symmetric).
(ii) Heat flows from hotter to colder places, so the ternary quadratic form (a11, a22, a33; a23, a31, a12) must be positive definite. This is written in Gauss's notation for ternary forms. In modern terms: the flux is q = -a grad u, and the condition q·grad u < 0 for grad u ≠ 0 means grad u^T a grad u > 0.

§3. Goal: rewrite (I) in arbitrary new independent variables s1, s2, s3.

Method (variational). Equation (I) is necessary and sufficient for the following: for arbitrary infinitesimal variation δu, the expression
(A) δ ∫∫∫ sum a_{ii'} u_{x_i} u_{x_i'} dx + ∫∫∫ 2h u_t δu dx
taken over the body depends only on the values of δu on the boundary.

Implicit step (mine): by symmetry of a,
δ∫ a_{ii'} u_i u_i' = 2∫ a_{ii'} u_i' (δu)_{x_i}.
Integrating by parts gives
2∮ (a grad u)·n δu dS − 2∫ div(a grad u) δu dx.
So (A) equals
2∮ (a grad u)·n δu dS − 2∫ [div(a grad u) − h u_t] δu dx.
The volume term vanishes for all δu iff (I) holds. (Note that u_t is not varied.)

Change of variables. By the chain rule, u_{x_i} = sum_mu u_{s_mu} ∂s_mu/∂x_i, and dx1dx2dx3 = ds1ds2ds3 / J, where J = Σ± ∂s1/∂x1 ∂s2/∂x2 ∂s3/∂x3 = det(∂s/∂x). Hence (A) becomes
(B) δ ∫∫∫ sum b_{mu nu} u_{s_mu} u_{s_nu} ds + ∫∫∫ 2k u_t δu ds,
with
b_{mu nu} = (sum_{i,i'} a_{ii'} ∂s_mu/∂x_i ∂s_nu/∂x_i') / J,
k = h / J.
In matrix form, b = S a S^T / J with S = ∂s/∂x. That is, a and h transform as a contravariant tensor density and a scalar density.

Because the boundary-only property is coordinate-free, the transformed equation is the Euler–Lagrange equation of (B):
sum_mu ∂/∂s_mu ( sum_nu b_{mu nu} u_{s_nu} ) = k u_t.
This is the same form as (I).

The page ends by introducing the determinants A, B of forms (1) a and (2) b, and their adjugate forms (α), (β), which are defined on the next page. There Riemann derives:
- A = B J;
- β = (∂x/∂s)^T α (∂x/∂s), i.e. sum α dx dx = sum β ds ds;
- h/A = k/B.
This reduces the problem to the equivalence of the quadratic differential form sum α_{ii'} dx_i dx_i' (the metric (a^{-1})·det a), which is later treated by Gauss's surface-theory method.
errors: No mathematical errors on this page.
Implicitly the Jacobian J is assumed positive (orientation-preserving change of variables); otherwise |J| should appear in dx = ds/|J|, and in b and k.

The equivalence 'equation (I) iff (A) depends only on boundary values of δu' is asserted without the integration-by-parts argument. It is standard and correct, given sufficient smoothness and symmetry of a.
Minor inconsistency in the source context: equation (I) on the previous page (as transcribed) has 'b' on the right-hand side, while this page calls the coefficient h.

results.what: Anisotropic inhomogeneous heat equation div(a grad u) = h u_t, with symmetric, positive-definite conductivity matrix justified physically (reciprocity; heat flows hot to cold)
results.modern_name: Anisotropic heat conduction with symmetric positive-definite conductivity tensor

results.what: Characterization of the PDE as the condition that the first variation of the energy-type integral plus the time term depends only on boundary values
Transformation law b = S a S^T / det S, k = h/det S of the coefficients under arbitrary curvilinear coordinates, obtained by transforming the variational integral
results.modern_name: Transformation of a contravariant 2-tensor density / Laplace–Beltrami operator in curvilinear coordinates
results.usually_credited_to: Jacobi (1832/1834, transformation of Laplace equation via variational integral), Lamé (curvilinear coordinates); this essay itself (Riemann 1861, publ. 1876)

deep.surprise_reason: This is the opening of Riemann's well-known 1861 Paris prize essay, published in his Gesammelte Werke (1876). The page contains only the standard setup: symmetric positive-definite conductivity, the variational characterization, and the transformation law of the coefficients. The famous content (curvature tensor, equivalence of quadratic forms) comes later.

checkable.asserts: The Euler–Lagrange expression of sum a_ij u_i u_j is -2 div(a grad u), so (A) has boundary-only variation iff div(a grad u) = h u_t

transcription_corrections: In (A) and (B) the variation δ applies only to the first triple integral; the second integral already contains δu explicitly (transcription is consistent with the image).
Previous page's equation (I) right-hand side should read h ∂u/∂t (this page names the coefficient h), not b ∂u/∂t.
The forms (a11, a22, a33; a23, a31, a12) are written in Gauss's two-row notation for ternary quadratic forms, not as matrices; a 2x3 'pmatrix' rendering could mislead.
